stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: An economist randomly selected 400 people from the list of everyone who filed for unemployment benefits in one state during 2025. Of these 400 people, 200 were randomly assigned to attend a weekly résumé workshop, and the other 200 were given no workshop. After six months, the workshop group had a significantly higher reemployment rate than the group with no workshop.
choices: The workshop is associated with higher reemployment for these 400 people, but it cannot be said to cause it.
The workshop causes higher reemployment for people who filed for unemployment benefits in that state during 2025.
The workshop causes higher reemployment for people who file for unemployment benefits in any state in any year.
The workshop causes higher reemployment for the 400 people studied, but the result cannot be extended beyond them.
explanation: Check both kinds of randomness. People were randomly assigned to the workshop or to no workshop, so you can draw a cause-and-effect conclusion. They were also randomly selected from everyone who filed in that state during 2025, so the conclusion extends to that population and no further.

A.why: You treated this like an observational study. The workshop was randomly assigned, so the study supports a causal claim, not just an association.

C.why: You stretched the conclusion past the population sampled. The 400 people came from one state in one year, so the result cannot be generalized to every state and every year.

D.why: You ignored the random selection. Because the 400 were randomly chosen from all 2025 filers in the state, the causal conclusion extends to that whole group, not just the people studied.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices: Zinc coating causes fewer corrosion cracks in steel bridges in the region.
Zinc coating causes fewer corrosion cracks in steel bridges everywhere.
Zinc coating is associated with fewer corrosion cracks only in the 150 bridges.
Zinc coating is associated with fewer corrosion cracks in the region's bridges.
explanation: The engineer only recorded which bridges already had a coating. Nothing was randomly assigned, so you can claim an association but not a cause. The bridges were randomly selected from all steel bridges in the region, so the association extends to the region's steel bridges.

A.why: You accepted a causal claim from observational data. The engineer did not decide which bridges got a coating, so other differences between the bridges could explain the cracks.

B.why: You made two mistakes: you claimed a cause from an observational study, and you generalized beyond the region the bridges were sampled from.

C.why: You overlooked the random selection. Because the 150 bridges were randomly drawn from all steel bridges in the region, the association can be extended to that whole population.

stimulus: At one clinic, 120 adults volunteered for a vaccine trial. Each volunteer was randomly assigned to receive either a vaccine made with a new adjuvant or the standard vaccine. Four weeks later, the group that received the new-adjuvant vaccine had significantly higher average antibody levels than the standard group.
choices: The new-adjuvant vaccine causes higher antibody levels among adults across the country.
The new-adjuvant vaccine causes higher antibody levels among people similar to the volunteers.
The new-adjuvant vaccine is associated with higher antibody levels but cannot be shown to cause them.
The new-adjuvant vaccine is associated with higher antibody levels among adults across the country.
explanation: The volunteers were randomly assigned to the two vaccines, so you can claim the new adjuvant causes the higher antibody levels. They were not randomly selected from any population, because they chose to volunteer at one clinic. That means the conclusion reaches only people similar to the volunteers. Choice B gets both parts right.

A.why: The causal part is right, but the volunteers weren't randomly selected from all adults in the country. Without random selection you can't generalize to that population.

C.why: This is the trap of mixing up the two kinds of randomness. A missing random sample limits who the result applies to. It doesn't block a causal claim, because random assignment is what permits cause, and this study used random assignment.

D.why: You made two errors. You settled for "associated" even though the treatments were randomly assigned, and you extended the result to the whole country without a random sample.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion based on this study?
stimulus: A meteorologist randomly selected 80 days from the past year in one coastal city. For each day, she recorded whether there was morning fog and the afternoon high temperature. The afternoon high averaged $58^\circ\text{F}$ on days with morning fog and $66^\circ\text{F}$ on days without it.
choices: In this city, morning fog causes afternoon highs to be about $8^\circ\text{F}$ lower.
In this city, morning fog is associated with afternoon highs about $8^\circ\text{F}$ lower.
In this city, morning fog is associated with afternoon highs about $8^\circ\text{F}$ higher.
In all coastal cities, morning fog is associated with afternoon highs about $8^\circ\text{F}$ lower.
explanation: The meteorologist only recorded what the weather already did. Nothing was randomly assigned, so you can claim an association but not a cause. The days were randomly selected from this one city's year, so the result applies to days in this city. The gap is $66 - 58 = 8^\circ\text{F}$, and fog days were the cooler ones.

A.why: You read a clear gap as proof that fog causes it. This is an observational study with no random assignment, so it can only show an association. Something else, such as cloud cover or wind off the ocean, could explain both the fog and the cooler afternoons.

C.why: You got the size of the gap right but flipped its direction. Fog days averaged $58^\circ\text{F}$, which is lower than the $66^\circ\text{F}$ on clear days, not higher.

D.why: The days came from a single city, so random selection only lets you generalize to days in that city. Extending the result to every coastal city goes beyond the population that was sampled.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion based on this study?
stimulus: A conservatory recruited 120 volunteer piano students. Half were randomly assigned to practice a new passage with a metronome, and the other half practiced it without one. In a later recording, the metronome group averaged 9 timing errors and the other group averaged 23.
choices: Among students like the volunteers, metronome practice causes about 14 fewer timing errors.
Among all piano students, metronome practice causes about 14 fewer timing errors.
Among students like the volunteers, metronome practice causes about 9 fewer timing errors.
Among students like the volunteers, metronome practice causes about 14 more timing errors.
explanation: The students were randomly assigned to the two practice methods, so you can claim a cause. They were volunteers, not a random sample of all piano students, so the conclusion only covers students like them. The gap is $23 - 9 = 14$ fewer errors for the metronome group.

B.why: You mixed up the two kinds of randomness. Random assignment supports the causal claim, but only random selection would let you generalize to all piano students, and these students were volunteers.

C.why: You used the metronome group's average, 9, instead of the gap between the groups. The difference is $23 - 9 = 14$.

D.why: You reversed which group did better. The metronome group made fewer errors (9) than the group without a metronome (23).

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion based on this study?
stimulus: A textile historian randomly selected 150 of the 3,000 nineteenth-century quilts in a museum's collection. On average, quilts sewn from naturally dyed fabric showed fading on 20% of their surface, and quilts sewn from synthetically dyed fabric showed fading on 35%.
choices: In this museum's collection, synthetic dyes caused about 15 percentage points more fading.
In this museum's collection, synthetic dyes are associated with about 15 percentage points more fading.
In this museum's collection, synthetic dyes are associated with about 35 percentage points more fading.
In all nineteenth-century quilts, synthetic dyes are associated with about 15 percentage points more fading.
explanation: The historian examined quilts that already existed and did not assign dyes to any of them, so the study can show an association but not a cause. The quilts were randomly selected from the museum's collection, so the result applies to that collection. The gap is $35\% - 20\% = 15$ percentage points.

A.why: You accepted a causal claim from observational data. No dyes were randomly assigned, so other differences between the two groups of quilts, such as age, fiber or how they were stored, could explain the fading.

C.why: You reported the synthetic-dye quilts' fading rate, 35%, instead of the gap between the two groups. The difference is $35 - 20 = 15$ percentage points.

D.why: The sample came only from this museum's collection, so it can't be generalized to every nineteenth-century quilt. Random selection reaches only as far as the population it was drawn from.
